To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) EMG activity is time-locked to the cycle in 4-month-olds, 2) EMG activity in 6-month-olds is time-locked and shows an anticipatory component, and 3) EMG activity of 8-month-olds is time locked and shows anticipatory and post-response components.

1) EMGs are more sensitive measures of interval timing than overt behavior in early development, and 2) the emergence of sub-threshold motor activity is an early indicator of the emergence of interval timing.
infants as young as 4 months of age are capable of producing interval timing, and that this timing emerges from the coupling of motor action and the perception of duration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the emergence of timing in early infancy and its relationship to action control.
the origins of interval timing and how the coupling of the action control and timing systems emerges during the first year of life.
the emergence of the coupling between action control and time perception in infancy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
interval timing in infancy is an embodied process.
infants are able to time intervals as early as 4 months, and that the coupling of action control and interval timing emerges early on in infancy.
the coupling between the motor system and the timing system is evident from the very beginning of life, and it emerges in the first months of postnatal development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
infants' motor system is already capable of timing intervals at the age of 4 months, and this ability emerges from an interaction between the infant and the caregiver, and is not an innate ability.
the coupling between action and time perception begins early in life and may even precede overt motor responses.
the coupling of timing and action emerges early in life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the origin of interval-timing is not a mystery, it is an emergent property of the motor system.
the origin of interval time perception is not to be found in the central nervous system, but in the action system.
the action control system is engaged in the earliest forms of interval timing.
